query: For high-entropy alloys intended for aerospace fasteners, what single intervention could improve the combination of mechanical durability, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence that supports it, and an experiment with clear results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A tailored thermomechanical treatment—specifically, a high degree of cold work (e.g., ~75% cold rolling) followed by a short, moderate-temperature aging step—will refine the microstructure and induce fine, beneficial precipitates in the high‐entropy alloy, thereby simultaneously enhancing mechanical durability, room‐temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance relative to the as-solution–treated state.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-solution–treated high-entropy alloy optimized for aerospace fasteners (for example, a Ti–Nb–Mo–Sn or similar alloy with a predominantly single-phase structure)
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to approximately 75% cold rolling to reduce grain size and introduce strain followed by a short precipitation hardening heat treatment (e.g., heating at around 350°C for 15 minutes) to induce fine and evenly dispersed secondary precipitates
generation.conditions: Room temperature mechanical testing, including nanoindentation creep tests in ambient atmosphere and corrosion evaluation in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution (or similar aggressive medium), mimicking service conditions for aerospace fasteners
generation.structural_mediator: Ultrafine grains and finely dispersed precipitates (e.g., metastable α or other strengthening phases) that not only block dislocation motion (improving yield strength and creep resistance) but also promote the formation of a uniform, protective passive oxide layer
generation.mechanism: The severe plastic deformation refines the grain structure and enhances dislocation density, while the subsequent aging triggers controlled precipitation hardening. These microstructural changes increase dislocation pinning (thereby reducing creep rate at room temperature) and improve the uniformity and stability of the passive film, which increases corrosion resistance. Together, these lead to improved mechanical durability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated (as-solution–treated) baseline, the treated alloy is expected to exhibit: (1) higher yield strength and improved durability due to grain refinement and precipitate strengthening; (2) a lower room-temperature creep rate due to dislocation pinning by fine precipitates; and (3) enhanced corrosion resistance as evidenced by higher polarization resistance and lower corrosion current density.
generation.baseline: An as-solution–treated high-entropy alloy that has a relatively coarser grain structure and lower dislocation/precipitate density, resulting in inferior strength, creep performance, and corrosion resistance
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected to hold under typical aerospace fastener service conditions at room temperature and under moderate corrosive exposures (e.g., saline environments). The effect may be less pronounced if the alloy has excessive precipitate coarsening or if service conditions deviate significantly in temperature or chemical aggressiveness.
generation.uncertainty: While prior work on similar alloys (e.g., the Ti80–Nb10–Mo5–Sn5 system) indicates that cold rolling and precipitation hardening can improve yield strength and corrosion resistance, the precise quantitative improvements in room-temperature creep resistance and the optimal processing parameters for the specific HEA composition intended for aerospace fasteners remain to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of aerospace fastener specimens from the same batch of the designated HEA. One set remains in the as-solution–treated (untreated) condition while the other set is subjected to 75% cold rolling followed by aging at ~350°C for 15 minutes. Conduct parallel testing of both sets.
measurements: Mechanical durability: Tensile tests to measure yield strength and ductility.
Room-temperature creep resistance: Nanoindentation creep tests to determine creep rate and creep strain rate sensitivity.
Corrosion resistance: Potentiodynamic polarization tests in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution to measure corrosion current density and polarization resistance.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated specimens do not show statistically significant improvements in yield strength, reduced creep rate, and enhanced corrosion resistance (i.e., lower corrosion current density and higher polarization resistance) compared to the untreated baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The microstructure, mechanical properties, and corrosion properties of the Ti80–Nb10–Mo5–Sn5 alloy were investigated under different conditions, including cold rolling and precipitation hardening treatment at various temperatures. The XRD patterns revealed that the alloy exhibited a single β phase in the solution-treated state. In contrast, the SIM transformation induced a β + α″ phase after cold rolling (50% and 75%), while heating at 350 °C for 15 min resulted in a β + α phase. Cold rolling significantly reduced the grain size of the β phase, while high-temperature precipitation hardening treatment led to larger grain sizes. Additionally, α precipitates were found in the ST sample after precipitation hardening treatment at room temperature for 30 days. After undergoing 75% cold rolling, the Ti80–Nb10–Mo5–Sn5 alloy (CR75) exhibited a significant increase in yield strength, albeit with a slight increase in elastic modulus. Moreover, the corrosion resistance of the Ti80–Nb10–Mo5–Sn5 alloy significantly increased after both the cold rolling and precipitation hardening treatments. Structural components used in high-temperature environments often fail due to high-temperature creep. Traditional creep tests, such as uniaxial tensile or compression tests, often require large sample sizes and long testing periods, which has limited the research on the creep properties of RHEAs. To overcome these limitations, the use of nanoindentation techniques for studying creep behavior offers an effective alternative. Nanoindentation is applying a small indentation load on the surface of the material to measure its mechanical properties, allowing for the assessment of creep properties at a very small scale. The advantages of this technique include the small size of samples required and short experimental periods.
